LESSON 90 OF 106·Defensive Operations: Detect, Respond, Recover

Logs and Telemetry: What to Collect and Why

Turning a question into a log source: what a defender needs to see, which log establishes what, and the collection mistakes that make good telemetry useless.

Applied Foundation17 min
Why this matters

Logs are the raw material of every investigation. The design question is not what you can log, but what you will need in six months when you do not yet know what you are looking for.

INTERACTIVE FLOW MODEL

  1. Vector: An attacker or faulty client alters parameters, headers, timing, or sequence order.

  3. Impact: The component trusts unverified data, crossing a confidentiality or integrity boundary.
01 Untrusted Input

  1. Verification: Centralise collection so host compromise cannot erase the record.
  2. Enforcement: Checks run deterministically on the server side for every sensitive action.
  3. Resilience: Invalid requests fail closed and emit structured security telemetry.

What you'll learn

  • How it works
  • The background
  • Real-world examples
  • What to look for

How it works

  • Collection is only useful if it survives the attack, so logs need to live somewhere the compromised host cannot reach.
  • Log integrity matters: an attacker who can edit a log can mislead the investigation.
  • Retention is a real trade-off between disk cost and the window in which you might need the data.
  • Time synchronisation decides whether records from different systems can be correlated at all.
  • Context matters as much as events: an event without the user, source and outcome is hard to act on.

The background

  • Local logging was controlled by whoever owned the machine, which meant an administrator could erase their tracks.
  • Central collection solved that and created a new problem: far more data than anyone reads.
  • Structured logging formats made cross-source correlation practical for the first time.
  • Current practice treats log data as a security asset with its own access controls and lifecycle.

Real-world examples

  • An investigation stalls because authentication records for the relevant week were never collected.
  • A system whose clock drifted produces a timeline that looks plausible and is wrong.
  • Logs stored on the same host as the compromised application are gone by the time anyone looks.

What to look for

  • Check which events are actually collected, and whether successful logins are included as well as failures.
  • Check whether a local administrator can delete or alter the logs you rely on.
  • Check the retention period against the longest window an investigation might realistically need.
  • Check clock synchronisation across every system whose records you intend to correlate.

Key takeaways

  • Centralise collection so host compromise cannot erase the record.
  • Log authentication, privilege changes, administrative actions and outbound connections, not just errors.
  • Synchronise time across systems, and treat drift as a monitoring alert.
  • Protect log storage with its own access controls and integrity checking.
  • Set retention deliberately and make it visible what is kept and for how long.
